```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6,
                      out.width = "100%", dpi = 150)
set.seed(2021)   # randomized quantile residuals
```

During the COVID-19 pandemic, German intensive care units reported every day how
many COVID-19 patients they were treating. For most of the pandemic they did
not report how many patients had arrived that day and how many had left, yet
planners needed both: arrivals tell you how fast the epidemic is reaching
hospitals, departures how long beds stay occupied. This article estimates the
two flows from the occupancy alone, following Rave and Kauermann (2025), and
then does what they could not: checks the estimates against admissions that the
register began to publish later.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(skellam)
library(ggplot2)
library(splines)
```

## Why a Skellam distribution

If $O_t$ is the number of patients in intensive care on day $t$, then

$$
O_t - O_{t-1} = A_t - D_t ,
$$

where $A_t$ counts the patients admitted and $D_t$ the patients who left
(discharged to a normal ward, moved elsewhere, or died). If $A_t$ and $D_t$ are
independent Poisson counts with rates $\lambda_{1t}$ and $\lambda_{2t}$, the
daily change has a Skellam distribution with mean $\lambda_{1t} - \lambda_{2t}$
and variance $\lambda_{1t} + \lambda_{2t}$. The mean alone tells you only the
net flow; the variance tells you how large the two flows are. A ward where ten
patients arrive and ten leave each day has the same mean change as one where one
arrives and one leaves, but its changes swing much more.

## The data

`icu_bavaria` contains the daily COVID-19 occupancy of adult intensive care in
Bavaria from the DIVI intensive care register, the infections reported in the
previous seven days, and, from 29 July 2021, the first admissions, all published
by the Robert Koch Institute under a CC BY 4.0 licence.

```{r data}
d <- icu_bavaria
d$change    <- c(NA, diff(d$occupancy))
d$occ_lag   <- c(NA, head(d$occupancy, -1))
d$weekday   <- factor(format(d$date, "%u"), levels = 1:7,   # %u: 1 = Monday
                      labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"))
head(d[!is.na(d$admissions), ], 3)
```

```{r occupancy, fig.cap = "COVID-19 patients in adult intensive care in Bavaria. The register reports first admissions from the dashed line on."}
ggplot(d, aes(date, occupancy)) +
  geom_line(colour = skellam_palette()[["fitted"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2021-07-29"), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = skellam_palette()[["neutral"]]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Patients") +
  theme_skellam()
```

A Skellam distribution with positive rates needs a variance at least as large
as the absolute mean. Month by month, the daily changes pass that test with a
wide margin, so both flows are clearly present:

```{r moments}
s <- subset(d, date >= as.Date("2021-08-01") & date <= as.Date("2023-06-30"))
m <- aggregate(change ~ format(date, "%Y-%m"), s,
               function(z) c(mean = mean(z), variance = var(z)))
m <- data.frame(month = m[[1]], m[[2]])
head(m, 6)
all(m$variance > abs(m$mean))
```

We work with August 2021 to June 2023, the period in which the reported
admissions let us check the results.

## A model for the two flows

Following Rave and Kauermann (2025), admissions depend on the infections
reported in the previous week and on the day of the week, and departures on the
day of the week. Both have a smooth trend in time, for the changes in testing,
variants and treatment that no covariate captures. One assumption is ours: each
patient in intensive care leaves with a daily probability that changes only
slowly, so the expected number of departures is proportional to yesterday's
occupancy. That enters the model as an offset, `offset(log(occ_lag))`. (Rave and
Kauermann used an offset built from past admissions and the distribution of
the length of stay instead.)

In `skellam.reg()` the part of the formula before `|` models $\lambda_1$, the
rate of the counts that are added (admissions), and the part after it
$\lambda_2$, the rate of the counts that are subtracted (departures).

```{r fit}
s$t <- as.numeric(s$date - min(s$date))
flows <- skellam.reg(change ~ log(cases7) + ns(t, 6) + weekday |
                       offset(log(occ_lag)) + ns(t, 6) + weekday, data = s)
round(coef(flows, "lambda1")[c("(Intercept)", "log(cases7)")], 3)
```

A 10% rise in reported infections goes with about
`r round(100 * (1.1^coef(flows, "lambda1")[["log(cases7)"]] - 1), 1)`% more
admissions. The weekday effects matter for both flows (likelihood-ratio test
against the same model without them):

```{r weekday}
no_weekday <- skellam.reg(change ~ log(cases7) + ns(t, 6) |
                            offset(log(occ_lag)) + ns(t, 6), data = s)
anova(no_weekday, flows)
```

The fitted departure rate per patient is the daily probability of leaving
intensive care, and its inverse is the mean length of stay:

```{r stay}
rates <- predict(flows, type = "rates")
leave <- rates[, "lambda2"] / s$occ_lag
c(daily_probability = mean(leave), mean_stay_days = 1 / mean(leave))
```

## Checking the estimates against reported admissions

Rave and Kauermann noted that they could not validate their estimates, because
admissions were not published. Since 29 July 2021 the register has reported
first admissions, so we can compare. The model never saw them.

```{r validate, fig.cap = "Weekly admissions estimated from the occupancy alone (blue) and first admissions reported by the hospitals (grey)."}
week <- as.Date(cut(s$date, "week"))
w <- data.frame(week = sort(unique(week)),
                estimated = as.vector(tapply(rates[, "lambda1"], week, sum)),
                reported  = as.vector(tapply(s$admissions, week, sum)))
c(correlation = cor(w$estimated, w$reported),
  ratio = sum(w$estimated) / sum(w$reported))

ggplot(w, aes(week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = reported, colour = "Reported first admissions")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = estimated, colour = "Estimated from occupancy")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Reported first admissions" = skellam_palette()[["observed"]],
                                 "Estimated from occupancy" = skellam_palette()[["fitted"]])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Admissions per week", colour = NULL) +
  theme_skellam() + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

For a model that sees only the net daily change, the agreement is good: the
estimates follow the reported admissions through most waves and match their
total within a few percent. The clear miss is February to April 2022, early in
the Omicron wave, when the estimates fall short by up to half. The smooth
trend, with six degrees of freedom over two years, may be too stiff to follow
how quickly the share of infections ending in intensive care changed then.

## How good is the fit?

The randomized quantile residuals of a correct model are standard normal.
Here their standard deviation is clearly above one:

```{r resid}
q <- residuals(flows, type = "quantile")
c(mean = mean(q), sd = sd(q))
```

The daily changes vary more than admissions and departures alone can explain.
The rest comes from movements the model does not describe: patients moved
between hospitals (who leave one unit and enter another, without being first
admissions), reports corrected the next day, units that miss a day.

This shows what can and cannot be learned from a difference. The data identify
the sum $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$ through the variance, so any extra variation is
read as extra flow unless the model rules that out. If the departure rate is
allowed to depend freely on occupancy, the fit improves and the residuals
become standard normal, but the estimated admissions then run well above the
reported ones:

```{r free}
free <- skellam.reg(change ~ log(cases7) + ns(t, 6) + weekday |
                      log(occ_lag) + ns(t, 6) + weekday, data = s)
compare <- function(m) {
  r <- predict(m, type = "rates")
  c(AIC = AIC(m), residual_sd = sd(residuals(m, type = "quantile")),
    admissions_ratio = sum(r[, "lambda1"]) / sum(s$admissions))
}
round(rbind(proportional = compare(flows), free = compare(free)), 2)
```

The two models answer different questions. The model with departures
proportional to occupancy estimates the patient flows; the free model describes
the distribution of the daily change, which is what a monitoring rule needs.
Its hanging rootogram shows observed and expected frequencies in close
agreement:

```{r rootogram, fig.cap = "Hanging rootogram of the free model: bars of observed counts hang from the expected counts; bars ending near zero mean a good fit."}
plot(free) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-40, 40))
```

## A monitoring rule

Surveillance systems flag counts that are unusually high for the time of year
and the current situation (Salmon, Schumacher and Höhle, 2016). The Skellam
quantile function gives such a rule for the daily change: flag a day when the
change falls outside the central 99% of its predicted distribution.

```{r monitor, fig.cap = "Daily change in occupancy with the central 99% interval of the free model; flagged days in orange."}
r <- predict(free, type = "rates")
s$lower <- qskellam(0.005, r[, "lambda1"], r[, "lambda2"])
s$upper <- qskellam(0.995, r[, "lambda1"], r[, "lambda2"])
s$flag  <- s$change < s$lower | s$change > s$upper
c(flagged = sum(s$flag), expected = round(0.01 * nrow(s), 1))

ggplot(s, aes(date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), fill = skellam_palette()[["band"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(y = change), size = 0.6, colour = skellam_palette()[["observed"]]) +
  geom_point(data = s[s$flag, ], aes(y = change), colour = skellam_palette()[["reference"]]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Change in occupancy") +
  theme_skellam()
```

The number of flagged days is close to the 1% expected by chance, so the rule is
calibrated. In practice the model would be fitted to past data only and the
interval computed one day ahead; here, for brevity, it is fitted to the whole
period.

## What this analysis leaves out

Rave and Kauermann work with all German districts, with age-specific infection
rates and spatial effects, and estimate the model with a stochastic EM
algorithm. This article uses one state and maximum likelihood with
`skellam.reg()`, which is enough to show the idea and to check it against the
admissions reported later. Like theirs, the model treats admissions and
departures as independent, which they justify by the absence of triage in
German intensive care.
